name: Facial exerciser

image.caption: facial exercises 1: Discover a Lovelier You (Woman Alive, 1972)

lead: Facial exercisers are small silicone or resistance devices placed in the mouth or on the cheeks to work the smile and cheek muscles, and are promoted alongside facial yoga routines. They are marketed for fuller cheeks, less sagging and a more youthful face.
The idea is to tone facial muscles the way gym training builds body muscle.

paras: Repeated contraction against resistance may enlarge or strengthen the facial muscles, increasing cheek volume in the area they cover. Whether this meaningfully changes how the face looks is less clear.

Overuse can cause muscle soreness, jaw tension or temporomandibular strain, and repeated expressions may deepen some lines. Evidence is limited: the main study was a small uncontrolled trial of facial exercise in middle-aged women with high dropout and a conflict of interest, showing modest cheek fullness improvement. No trial tested the devices themselves.

lead: Facial exercisers are small silicone or resistance devices held in the mouth or against the cheeks to work the smile, cheek and jaw muscles. They are sold alongside facial yoga routines and marketed for fuller cheeks, less sagging and a more youthful or more defined face. The underlying idea is that repeated contraction against resistance may strengthen or enlarge facial muscles, as strength training does elsewhere in the body.

No published trial has tested a commercial facial exerciser device for appearance. Research on facial exercise as a technique is limited: a 2014 systematic review found that all nine included studies reported positive outcomes but none used a control group or randomization, and concluded that the evidence was insufficient to judge effectiveness.[1] A 2018 single-arm study of a 20-week facial exercise program in middle-aged women reported modest improvement in cheek fullness and estimated age.[2] A 2024 case report of a jaw exerciser found no change in two users.
Facial exercise is also an established part of rehabilitation for facial palsy, which is a separate use.

paras: Devices include mouth-held silicone trainers that the user bites or presses with the lips, resistance bands for the cheeks, and jaw exercisers. They are usually accompanied by routines of repeated holds or reps, much like facial yoga.

The claimed mechanism is that resisted contraction increases the size or tone of facial muscles, so that the face looks fuller or firmer. The 2018 study authors measured outcomes with photographic aging scales rather than direct muscle measurements.[2] Whether this changes appearance meaningfully has not been established, and the authors of the jaw-exerciser case report argued that the chewing muscles targeted by such devices do not directly affect submental fat, jaw structure or skin elasticity.
No studies found of commercial facial exercise devices for appearance outcomes. Related research on facial exercise as a technique follows.

A 2014 systematic review in Aesthetic Surgery Journal identified nine reports of facial exercises for facial rejuvenation. All reported positive outcomes, but they were case reports, small case series or single-group before-and-after studies, and most assessments were subjective and unblinded. The authors concluded that the evidence was insufficient to determine effectiveness and that large randomized trials were needed.[1]

In a 2018 research letter in JAMA Dermatology, 27 adults aged 40 to 65 enrolled in a 20-week single-arm study of a 32-exercise program, and 16 women completed it. Blinded raters scored upper cheek fullness from 1.8 to 1.1 and lower cheek fullness from 1.6 to 0.9 on photoscales, and estimated mean age fell from 50.8 to 48.1 years; other measures did not change significantly. Limitations included the small sample, high dropout, no control group and lack of blinding of participants and administrators. One author founded the company whose regimen was used, and the study was funded by departmental funds.[2]

A 2024 case report of two men who used a commercially available jaw exerciser for about three months found no change in double chin, jawline or neck tightness in photographs, with no objective measurements. Both participants were also authors.

Systematic reviews and Cochrane reviews have examined facial exercise and physical therapy for facial palsy (Bell's palsy).[3][4] Randomized trials have also studied post-injection facial exercise with botulinum toxin and face yoga in temporomandibular dysfunction.[5][6] These address function or treatment response rather than cosmetic rejuvenation.

No safety studies of commercial facial exercisers have been published. Commonly reported issues are muscle soreness, jaw tension and gagging with intraoral devices; users in the jaw-exerciser case report reported dissatisfaction with gagging and suction.

Facial exercise devices are discussed with jaw and cheek training routines as non-invasive ways to improve facial contour. The only controlled-style evidence is the small 2018 study of an exercise program rather than a device.

timeline.event: Systematic review finds evidence on facial exercises for rejuvenation insufficient.[1]
JAMA Dermatology research letter reports modest cheek-fullness improvement in a single-arm facial exercise study.[2]
Case report finds no change with a commercial jaw exerciser.
